Triggers.value: Being in a locked or confined room

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad
I dwell on what I have done wrong
I go over and over the details of the event trying to make sense of it

Threat.value: I feel on guard even inside my own home
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong

Negative Appraisals.value: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable.
You can never know who will harm you

vignette:
Marisol Alvarez is a 59-year-old divorced Latina woman who works as a project manager for a mid-sized construction firm, a role that once suited the part of her that had been organized, practical, and steady under pressure. She traces the change in herself to a period of captivity several years ago, when a man she knew through work lured her to an empty property under the pretense of reviewing a schedule problem. Instead, he locked her inside a small storage room at the back of the building and kept her there for hours. The room had no windows and barely enough space for her to sit with her back against the wall. At one point, when she tried to force the door and twist away as he restrained her, she wrenched her neck sharply. She remembers the pain blooming there and then spreading into a rigid, burning ache while she realized she could not get out. What remains most vivid is not a single image but the sense of having no options: the locked door, the stale air, the certainty that no one would hear her if she shouted, and the humiliating knowledge that another person had complete control over whether she stayed trapped.

In the months after, Marisol did not speak about the captivity in a straightforward way. She would catch herself saying it had not really happened the way she remembered, or that perhaps it was not as bad as she made it out to be. At other times she became absorbed in reviewing every detail, trying to determine the exact moment she had made the wrong choice. She went over the phone call that got her there, the route she took, the first instant she noticed something was off, as if enough analysis might produce a different ending. When those loops intensified, they often turned into self-accusation. She would lie awake dwelling on what she had done wrong, asking herself why she had gone in, why she had not seen the danger sooner, why she had not said or done something that would have prevented the whole thing. These thoughts did not resolve anything, but they consumed long stretches of time and left her feeling depleted.

Her daily life narrowed in ways that made sense to her, even as they cost her. At work, being a project manager meant site visits, elevators in unfinished buildings, conference rooms with heavy doors, and long planning meetings in interior offices. She began hovering near exits and choosing the chair closest to the door. If a meeting room felt too enclosed, she found reasons to step out or reschedule. When a facilities problem once caused an electronic lock to stick for less than a minute, Marisol’s whole body surged into alarm; she was abruptly certain she was trapped again, her heart racing before anyone else in the room even understood there was a problem. Neck pain could do something similar. A simple flare after a long day at the computer would instantly pull her back to the storage room, and she would become tense and watchful for the rest of the evening. Colleagues noticed she was more rigid and less available, and she knew her team now saw her as hard to approach.

At home she did not feel restored. She checked doors repeatedly and remained on guard even in her own apartment, listening for sounds in the hallway and staying alert to any shift in the lock. She told herself she knew she was safe, yet she could not relax into that knowledge. Her body reacted before her mind could catch up. A neighbor rattling the wrong doorknob, the click of a deadbolt, even realizing she had shut herself into the laundry room could bring a burst of fear so sudden that she felt embarrassed afterward. She has come to believe that you can never know who will harm you, because the person who confined her had seemed ordinary enough until he wasn’t. That conclusion has spread beyond the event itself into a broader mistrust that leaves her scanning people’s motives, including those of men at work and even acquaintances she has known for years.

What troubles Marisol almost as much as the fear is the sense that something essential in her has gone flat. She says she used to be a happy person, someone who laughed easily and took pride in keeping complicated projects moving. Now she experiences herself as miserable most of the time, and when family members try to draw her out, she often feels nothing at all. “Dead inside” is how she puts it, not dramatically but with resignation. After months of trying to manage on her own, she sought help when a routine planning meeting was moved to a windowless records room during an office renovation. As the door shut and she felt the familiar neck pain stiffen across her shoulders, she froze, then abruptly walked out in front of her staff. The incident left her shaken and ashamed. Coming to treatment, she is afraid that this reaction can happen anywhere and with anyone, and she hopes, cautiously, that she might find some way to feel like herself again rather than living as if danger is always one locked door away.
